title: Why Do Dogs Get Separation Anxiety? (And How To Actually Help)
description:
Does your dog panic, bark, or destroy things the second you leave the house? That's separation anxiety, and it's one of the most common (and misunderstood) dog behavior problems. In this video we break down why it happens and what actually helps.

script: Does your dog completely lose it the second you grab your keys? Barking, pacing, scratching at the door, sometimes even destroying furniture while you're gone? That's not your dog being bad. That's separation anxiety, and it's one of the most common behavior problems in dogs today. Here's what's really going on. Dogs are pack animals. For thousands of years, being separated from the group meant real danger. So when you walk out that door, some dogs' brains genuinely interpret it as a threat, not an inconvenience. Their stress hormones spike almost immediately, and that panic has to go somewhere, which is why you come home to chewed shoes or a trashed couch. The mistake most owners make is trying to fix this with punishment. That only adds more anxiety to a dog that's already overwhelmed. What actually works is building independence gradually. Start with leaving for just thirty seconds, then a few minutes, slowly stretching the time so your dog learns that you always come back. Pair your departures with something calming, like a stuffed treat toy, so alone time starts to feel safe instead of scary. And keep your goodbyes boring. No dramatic exits, no big emotional hellos. The calmer you are about leaving, the calmer your dog will learn to be too.
